findings.asked: Six-mark QWC on the root hair cell: structure, what it takes in and how.
findings.wentWrong: Most scored four or more, but only the better answers linked mineral absorption to active uptake; some claimed water is taken in by active transport, and a few called it a 'hair root cell'.
findings.rule: Minerals in by active transport; water in by osmosis; the extension gives a large surface area.

findings.asked: Explain a fertiliser run-off problem and put the stages of eutrophication in order.
findings.wentWrong: Answers that said 'nutrients' instead of nitrate or phosphate earned nothing for that point, and the order of the stages was widely confused - a strongly discriminating question.
findings.rule: Name the ion (nitrate/phosphate) and learn the stages as a causal chain.

findings.asked: Identify a root hair cell from a drawing, then describe and explain active transport.
findings.wentWrong: The cell had to be recognised by its lack of an extension (descriptions in terms of body parts were not accepted); active transport explanations went wrong on the direction of the concentration gradient, and again some said water enters by active transport.
findings.rule: Active transport moves mineral ions against the gradient (low to high) using energy from respiration.

findings.asked: Complete a diagram of the stages of eutrophication.
findings.wentWrong: Most earned something, but the last three stages (decomposers multiply, oxygen used up, animals die) were the ones left wrong or blank.
findings.rule: The end of the chain is about oxygen: bacteria respire, oxygen falls, fish die.

ruleToRemember: Roots take in mineral ions by active transport (against the gradient, energy from respiration) and water by osmosis. Eutrophication in order: fertiliser (nitrate/phosphate) washed into water, algae bloom, light blocked so plants die, bacteria decompose them and respire, oxygen runs out, animals die.
aStarSignal: Writing each eutrophication stage with its cause ('plants die because the algae block the light'), and naming the ion rather than 'nutrients'.
